content: The trachea, commonly referred to as the windpipe, is a tubular structure with an internal diameter of approximately 20–25 mm and a length of about 10–16 cm in humans. It begins at the larynx, located at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra (C6), and bifurcates into the primary (main) bronchi at the level of the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae (T4/T5). In mammals, this bifurcation allows air to pass into the lungs, while in birds, the trachea extends from the pharynx to the syrinx, facilitating airflow to the lungs. The trachea is lined with pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, which contains goblet cells that produce mucus. This mucus traps inhaled foreign particles, and the cilia propel these particles upward toward the larynx and pharynx, where they can be swallowed into the stomach for disposal. This mechanism is essential for maintaining a clean and functional airway. In humans, the trachea is reinforced by approximately 15–20 incomplete C-shaped cartilaginous rings. These rings provide structural support to the anterior and lateral walls of the trachea, ensuring that the airway remains open. The posterior part of the trachea, where the cartilaginous rings are incomplete, is connected by a band of smooth muscle known as the trachealis muscle. This muscle can contract to reduce the diameter of the tracheal lumen, thereby increasing airflow velocity during coughing to expel irritants or mucus. The esophagus lies posterior to the trachea. The incomplete nature of the cartilaginous rings allows the trachea to slightly collapse when food passes through the esophagus, preventing obstruction. The epiglottis, a flap-like structure, closes over the trachea during swallowing to prevent ingested material from entering the airway. Clinically, the trachea is significant in procedures such as endotracheal intubation, where an artificial tube is inserted into the trachea to secure an airway and facilitate ventilation of the lungs. Another procedure, tracheotomy, involves creating an opening in the anterior neck that extends into the tracheal lumen. A tracheostomy tube is then inserted through this opening, bypassing the larynx and vocal cords, to provide an alternative airway. Additional anatomical images and diagrams often accompany descriptions of the trachea, including cross-sections of the neck at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra, anterior views of the heart and lungs, the tracheobronchial lymph nodes, and various views of the larynx and its associated muscles and ligaments. These images also include transverse and sagittal sections of the trachea, as well as depictions of the esophagus in relation to the trachea in the cervical region and posterior mediastinum.
